points.label: A model is a learned function
points.description: The learner states that a model is a function or mapping that takes inputs (features) and produces outputs (predictions), and that this mapping is learned from data rather than hand-coded rule by rule.

points.label: Parameters encode what was learned
points.description: The learner explains that a model contains adjustable parameters (weights, coefficients) whose values are set during training, and that these parameter values are what store the learned patterns.

points.label: A model approximates, it does not memorize truth
points.description: The learner states that a model is an approximation of the real-world relationship fitted from limited data, so its predictions can be wrong, especially on inputs unlike its training data.

misconceptions.summary: A model is a database that looks up the answer it saw during training.
misconceptions.correction: The learner explains that a model generalizes rather than looks up: it compresses training data into parameters and can produce predictions for inputs it has never seen, unlike a lookup table which only returns stored entries.

misconceptions.summary: Once a model is trained, its predictions are objective facts.
misconceptions.correction: The learner clarifies that model outputs are estimates shaped by the training data and modeling choices; they carry uncertainty and inherit any biases or gaps in the data, so they should not be treated as guaranteed truth.

beginner: When people say 'the model', what physically is it? A program? A file? A bunch of numbers?
How is a model different from a normal program a developer writes with if-else rules?
confident: A trained model basically memorizes all its training examples and matches new inputs to the closest one it stored.
If a model is 95% accurate on training data, it will be 95% accurate on anything you give it.
skeptic: If a model is just an approximation fitted to past data, why should I trust it on data from next year when the world has changed?
Two teams can train different models on the same data and get different answers. Doesn't that show the whole thing is arbitrary?
